events.title: The Concordat of Worms
events.shortBlurb: At Worms, pope and emperor traded ring and sceptre for peace, closing the half-century Investiture Contest…
body: The struggle begun when Gregory VII forbade lay investiture in 1075 had outlived that pope and the emperor he humbled at Canossa. On 23 September 1122, at Worms on the Rhine, Pope Callixtus II and the Emperor Henry V set their names to the two declarations — the first concordat between the Church and a temporal power — that ended it.

The emperor renounced investiture with ring and crosier, the bestowal of spiritual office by a lay hand, and granted that elections should be canonical and consecration free. The pope conceded that in Germany elections might be held in the emperor's presence, and that the elect should receive the regalia by the touch of the sceptre — in Germany before consecration, in Burgundy and Italy within six months after.

The First Lateran Council ratified the concordat the following March. Its distinction of the spiritual sword from the temporal became the pattern of every later settlement between altar and throne, and the Church had won, at parchment's length, the freedom of her bishops.
